title: A cruising airplane holds speed when thrust matches drag
summary: NASA Glenn says a cruising airplane flies at a constant airspeed because thrust exactly balances drag, so the net force is zero.
body: NASA Glenn's aircraft page on the first law, last updated 21 July 2022, names four forces on an airplane: lift, weight, thrust, and drag. At constant altitude the guide sets lift and weight aside. A cruising aircraft then flies at constant airspeed because thrust exactly balances drag. There is no net force, and the airplane travels at constant velocity in a straight line. If the pilot adds thrust, the balance breaks, speed rises, and drag grows until the two match again at a higher speed.

sources.title: Aircraft Motion - Newton's First Law
sources.author: Nancy Hall, NASA Glenn Research Center
sources.note: Public-domain NASA Glenn page, last updated 21 July 2022. Paraphrase of the cruise example: thrust balances drag, constant velocity, and drag rising with speed.
